column2: Why can a small brainstem lesion produce crossed findings?
column3: It damages cranial-nerve nuclei or fascicles on its own side while also interrupting long tracts that serve the opposite side of the body.

column3: Beyond the cochlear nuclei, auditory fibres project bilaterally through the superior olivary complex and higher relays, so each ear is represented on both sides.

column2: Why can a small upper-brainstem lesion impair consciousness when a unilateral cortical lesion usually does not?

column2: How does the anatomy of lateral medullary syndrome explain its combination of signs?
column3: Damage to vestibular nuclei, inferior cerebellar peduncle, nucleus ambiguus, spinal trigeminal, spinothalamic and sympathetic fibres gives vertigo, ipsilateral ataxia, dysphagia, hoarseness and Horner syndrome.
